source_references.locator: 1 Introduction; 2 Data reduction; 2.1 A priori calibration; 2.2 Minispiral calibration test; 3 Results; 3.1 Light curves extraction; 3.2 Time lags; 3.2.1 Peak-time method; 3.2.2 Locally normalized cross-correlation function; 4 Discussion; 5 Conclusions; References; Introduction; Frequency-dependent time delays in Sgr A from a broadband VLA observation; Instructions for reporting errors
source_references.description: Complete, revision-matched arXiv TeX source package

analysis.reason: This VLA study quantifies a recurring frequency-dependent radio lag in Sgr A* and links it to a mildly relativistic outflow, which is relevant to compact-object jet timing but is outside the group's core FRB, supernova-engine, and dispersion-measure problems.
analysis.result: One broad brightening is present across $\sim 13$–$36\,\mathrm{GHz}$, with the maximum later at lower frequency. Peak-time and LCCF slopes agree at $\mathcal{S}\sim 40\,\mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}$: excluding the reference, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm peak}=41.2\pm 10.2\,\mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}$ and $\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCCF}=40.4\pm 5.8\,\mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}$. Checks give $\mathcal{S}_{\rm peak}=46.7\pm 8.0$, $42.3\pm 10.8$, and $40.9\pm 10.6\,\mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}$. The Ka-to-lowest-Ku peak lag is $81.1\pm 12.5\,\mathrm{min}$, while the lowest Ku LCCF lag is $58.4\pm 12.1\,\mathrm{min}$. These match earlier slopes $42\pm 14$ and $40.3\pm 2.0\,\mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}$ and are associated with outward motion at $\gamma\beta\sim 0.5$–$1.2$, without uniquely separating a jet from adiabatic synchrotron expansion.
analysis.problem: Sgr A* radio variations usually lead at higher frequency, but it is unresolved whether the delay comes from a jet, an expanding plasma, or magnetic-flux eruption and whether the positive delay–wavelength trend recurs.
analysis.method: A $\sim 6\,\mathrm{h}$ VLA A-configuration track on 2022 May 28 covers Ku/K/Ka (effective $\sim 13$–$36\,\mathrm{GHz}$). Stokes $I$ light curves are taken from visibility real parts on baselines $>150\,\mathrm{k}\lambda$, median-normalized, $1\,\mathrm{min}$ binned, and smoothed with a FWHM $7\,\mathrm{min}$ Gaussian; lags use peak times and an LCCF on $100$–$290\,\mathrm{min}$ with $50\%$ Monte Carlo errors. The minispiral test fits $V(t)=S_1(t)V^{\rm ext}+S_2(t)V^{\rm compact}$ on $<150\,\mathrm{k}\lambda$. Because $S_1(t)$ varies by $\sim 30$–$50\%$ with no systematic trend, amplitudes rely on 3C 286 and phase self-calibration. The extended-emission index is $S_\nu\propto\nu^\alpha$.
limits: In-field minispiral amplitude calibration was not used because extended A-configuration $(u,v)$ coverage at minispiral scales is sparse and the scale factors are unstable.
citation_leads: Frequency-dependent time delays in Sgr A from a broadband VLA observation: “with the maximum occurring progressively later at lower observing frequencies”
2.2 Minispiral calibration test: “In all cases, $S_{1}(t)$ exhibited strong variation of $\sim 30-50\%$, with no clear systematic trend.”
4 Discussion: “The peak-time method and LCCF analyses both find that the higher-frequency light curves lead the lower-frequency ones.”
5 Conclusions: “not be applied to the final lag analysis because the extended A configuration provides sparse $(u,v)$ coverage”
analysis.research_progress: The 2022 epoch reconfirms a stable positive slope $\mathcal{S}\sim 40\,\mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}$, consistent with measurements over more than 15 years and with a mildly relativistic outflow $\gamma\beta\sim 0.5$–$1.2$. The introduction separately quotes $\gamma\beta\sim 2$, $M\simeq 4\times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$, a $\sim 230\,\mathrm{GHz}$ ring, and a $1$–$2\,\mathrm{THz}$ self-absorption peak; the new scaling still does not identify a unique emission geometry.

The solid curves show the smoothed light curves, and the dashed vertical lines mark the corresponding peak times.
figures.label: Fig. 2

The solid curves show the smoothed light curves, the dashed vertical lines mark the measured peak times, and the shaded $\pm 7$ min regions indicate the visual peak-time windows. analysis.reason: The two late TDE radio rebrightenings give quantitative outflow, jet, and circumstellar-density constraints relevant to relativistic outflows and CSM interaction, but they are incremental relative to the group's core FRB, supernova-engine, and neutrino focus.
analysis.result: AT2019ehz ($z=0.074$) rebrightens at 1545 d, and its secondary flare is attributed to a second outflow launched near $1000$ d (linear $R_{\rm eq}$ extrapolation $1071^{+62}_{-79}$ d), with mean $\bar{\beta}=v/c$ rising from $0.003$ to $0.033$. AT2019eve ($z=0.081$) rebrightens at 1594 d with $L\sim6.7\times10^{38}$–$1\times10^{39}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, about $2$–$3\times$ the earlier $3.6\times10^{38}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, while $\nu_p$ rises from $1.6$ to $2.8\,\mathrm{GHz}$ at $F_{\nu,p}\sim1.0\,\mathrm{mJy}$. Its $R_{\rm eq}$ appears to fall by ${\sim}8\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{cm}$ over ${\sim}1000$ d; $\beta\lesssim0.06$ does not reach the off-axis-jet value $\beta_{\rm eq,N}=0.44$. Under a prompt launch, $E\sim7\times10^{48}\,\mathrm{erg}$ while $v$ declines from $0.06c$ to $0.02c$. Sample densities scale from $(R/R_s)^{-1}$ to $(R/R_s)^{-2}$; AT2019ehz is on average $\propto R^{-2}$ and AT2019eve $\propto R^{-1}$.
analysis.problem: The paper asks what produces secondary radio flares $\approx1550$–$1600$ d after optical TDE discovery—variable CSM, a decelerating off-axis jet, a delayed accretion-driven outflow, or a repeating partial TDE—especially when AT2019eve's synchrotron peak frequency rises instead of falling.

source_references.description: Complete, revision-matched arXiv TeX source package

analysis.reason: This MHD-PIC study of self-regulated cosmic-ray electron DSA at a high-Mach quasi-parallel shock is useful for SNR shock spectra and magnetic amplification, but it is not directly about FRBs, central engines, shock breakout, jets, or neutrinos.
analysis.result: Across supplied CRe mass fractions, the upstream magnetic pressure saturates at a common level $\langle B^{2}\rangle/B_{0}^{2}\approx 12$; increasing $\eta$ mainly shortens the time to saturation. Despite $r_{\rm tot}\simeq 5$, for which $q_p=3r/(r-1)=3.75$, the high-energy spectrum stays near the test-particle form $4\pi f(p)p^{4}=\mathrm{const}$ ($q_p=4$) rather than forming a concave NLDSA spectrum. The resolved-tail effective pressure converges to $P_{\rm CR}^{\rm eff}\sim 0.3\rho_0 v_0^2$ for $p/p_0\simeq 100$–$1000$, while low-momentum normalizations retain a strong $\eta$ dependence.
analysis.reading_entry: III.1 Self-regulation via saturation of a Bell-type instability in MHD-PIC
analysis.problem: Efficient DSA is predicted to build a smooth CR-pressure precursor that hardens the spectrum above the strong-shock test-particle slope $f(p)\propto p^{-4}$, yet observations favor $4\pi f(p)p^{4}=\mathrm{const}$ or steeper spectra.
analysis.method: Non-relativistic quasi-parallel shocks with $M_{\rm A}=M_s=50$ are evolved in Athena MHD-PIC: the thermal plasma is ideal MHD, CRe are macroparticles with $\bm{\mathcal{E}}=-({\bm v}_g\times{\bm B})/c$ and feedback $-{\bm F}_{\rm CR}$, and the control parameter is the supplied CRe mass fraction $\eta$ rather than a fixed injection efficiency. Self-regulation is measured through saturation of the electron-driven Bell mode and the resulting SLAMS-dominated upstream.
limits: Bell-generated SLAMS keep the CR pressure gradient, momentum deposition, and heating local to the shock, so the run does not realize a broad smooth NLDSA precursor.
citation_leads: Self-Regulated Cosmic-Ray Electron Acceleration in High-Mach-Number MHD-PIC Shocks: “These predictions are in tension with observations, which favor spectra closer to the test-particle form”
III.1 Self-regulation via saturation of a Bell-type instability in MHD-PIC: “The upstream magnetic pressure grows rapidly and saturates at $\langle B^{2}\rangle/B_{0}^{2}\approx 12$”
III.2 Spectral shape: “The downstream spectra retain a strong dependence on the supplied CRe fraction at low momenta”
III.2 Spectral shape: “while their high-energy normalizations converge at late times”
IV Discussion: “In this picture, upstream confinement by Bell-generated SLAMS concentrates the pressure buildup”
analysis.research_progress: The incremental result is a common self-regulated state: Bell-driven SLAMS scatter CRe and cap the coherent upstream current, so $\langle B^{2}\rangle/B_{0}^{2}\approx 12$ and the late high-energy normalization become insensitive to $\eta$. Fluid modification reaches $r_{\rm tot}\simeq 5$ but does not extend to the diffusion length of the highest-energy particles, leaving $p^{4}f\approx\mathrm{const}$ instead of the concave spectrum expected from $q_p=3r/(r-1)$.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Example of upstream magnetic field evolution and CRe energy phase space for the $\eta=0.25\%$ 1D run. Left column: magnetic field components $B_{x}/B_{0}$, $B_{y}/B_{0}$, and $B_{z}/B_{0}$ as functions of distance from the shock, $x-x_{\rm sh}$, at $t=32\Omega_{ci}^{-1}$ (a), $62\Omega_{ci}^{-1}$ (c), and $90\Omega_{ci}^{-1}$ (e). Right column: corresponding CRe energy phase-space density $Ef(E)$, with energy normalized to $E_{\rm sh}$ (b, d, f). The vertical line marks the shock position, shown in black in the left panels and white in the right panels. The upstream turbulence evolves from coherent, gyroradius-scale fluctuations at early times to intermittent, large-amplitude SLAMS in the nonlinear stage, which strongly scatter particles and produce sharp breaks in the upstream phase-space distribution.
figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.physical_core: Displays the temporal evolution of upstream magnetic field components ($B_x/B_0, B_y/B_0, B_z/B_0$) and corresponding cosmic-ray electron (CRe) energy phase-space density $Ef(E)$ as functions of distance from the shock ($x-x_{\rm sh}$). It captures the core physical transition from linear, gyroradius-scale coherent fluctuations into intermittent, large-amplitude SLAMS that scatter particles and induce sharp breaks in upstream phase space.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Magnetic field fluctuations, $\sqrt{B^{2}/\langle B^{2}\rangle}$ (color), and magnetic field lines (black lines) near the shock at a late stage of the evolution, $400\Omega^{-1}_{ci}$. Panels (a)–(d) show runs with increasing initial CRe mass fraction $\eta$. The arrow in panel (d) indicates the initial magnetic-field direction, inclined by $30\deg$ to the shock normal.
figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.physical_core: Presents the late-stage ($400\Omega_{ci}^{-1}$) two-dimensional spatial distribution of magnetic field fluctuations $\sqrt{B^2/\langle B^2\rangle}$ and magnetic field lines near the shock across different supplied CRe mass fractions $\eta$, showing the saturated structural response and field line distortion driven by CR feedback.

analysis.reason: This is a quantitative hard-state neutron-star X-ray study linking a 30 keV Suzaku feature in Aql X-1 to rp-process ashes, so it is relevant to compact-object high-energy observations, but it does not address FRBs, supernova engines, jets, neutrinos, shocks, or dispersion measure.
analysis.result: The hard-state hump is fit by a radiative-recombination redge with $E_{\rm K}=27\pm 1$ keV and $kT_{\rm e}=11^{+10}_{-5}$ keV; after gravitational redshift this corresponds to $Z\approx 48$–49. The weighted equivalent width is $\overline{\rm EW}=5.6\pm 1.9$ keV. Matching the flux requires $n_{\rm x}n_{\rm e}V\sim 3\times 10^{53}\,{\rm cm^{-3}}$ and $n_{\rm x}/n_{\rm H}\gtrsim 8\times 10^{-4}$, or $X_{\rm x}\gtrsim 0.06(A_{\rm x}/100)(X_{\rm H}/0.73)$, roughly $\sim 10^{7}$ times the solar Cd abundance. One-zone rp-process models favor stable ${}^{106}{\rm Cd}$, with a mass fraction up to 38% and survival for $\gtrsim 10$ days; convective mixing gives $\tau\equiv\Delta M_0/\dot{M}\sim 10^{7}\,{\rm s}$.
analysis.reading_entry: II The Spectral feature around 30 keV
analysis.problem: The issue is whether the approximately 30 keV hard-state hump in Aql X-1 is a radiative-recombination quasi-continuum from highly ionized Cd or In produced by the rp-process, despite the observed strength greatly exceeding that expected for solar Cd abundance.
analysis.method: Suzaku spectra are modeled with tbabs ($N_{\rm H}=0.36\times 10^{22}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$), a blackbody, CompPS thermal Comptonization, an Fe K line, and a redge; Gaussian equivalent widths are compared with an expected K$\alpha$ cascade near $0.75E_{\rm K}$. Atmospheric constraints use $H=kT_{\rm e}/(m_{\rm i}g)$ and $\Phi_{\rm rec}=n_{\rm x}n_{\rm e}V\int_{E_{\rm K}}^{\infty}S(E)dE$. One-zone bursts use JINA Reaclib, while post-burst retention is tested with Taylor–Spruit mixing and dilution.
assumptions: Heavy-element ions producing the redge must be nearly fully ionized, with an ionization temperature much higher than the ambient 11 keV electrons.
limits: The estimated Cd/In residence time exceeds 10 days independently of $\alpha$ only for the adopted accretion rate $\dot{M}\sim 0.01\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$.
citation_leads: II The Spectral feature around 30 keV: “The best-fit K-edge energy was $E_{\rm K}=27\pm 1$ keV”
III.3 Ionization of heavy elements: “they must be nearly fully ionized, requiring that their ionization temperature is much higher”
IV Comparison with Nucleosynthesis calculations for X-ray bursts: “the most likely origin of the 30 keV feature observed from Aql X-1”
V How to lift up the Cd ion?: “Therefore, the Cd/In can remain in the convective atmosphere for more than 10 days, regardless of $\alpha$ values.”
analysis.research_progress: The paper advances the 30 keV Aql X-1 hump from a phenomenological feature to a specific rp-ash candidate: ${}^{106}{\rm Cd}$ can supply the required heavy-element fraction, while magnetic turbulent mixing can keep Cd/In in the convective atmosphere for more than 10 days, with $\tau\equiv\Delta M_0/\dot{M}\sim 10^{7}\,{\rm s}$.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) The combined D2–D4 spectrum, shown together with the best-fit model that includes a redge component and an additional Gaussian for the cascade K $\alpha$ line at $\sim 20$ keV. (b) Residuals from the canonical continuum model (for reference). (c) Same as (b) but with the redge component added to the model. (d) Fit residuals from the best-fit model shown in panel (a).
figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.physical_core: Combined Suzaku D2–D4 X-ray spectrum of Aquila X-1 fitted with the canonical continuum plus a radiative recombination edge (redge) at $\sim 30\text{ keV}$ and an associated cascade $K\alpha$ Gaussian emission line at $\sim 20\text{ keV}$, demonstrating clear residual reduction across panels (b)–(d).

figures.caption: Figure 2: A diagram of hydrogen number density, $n_{H}$, versus that of Cd, $n_{x}$, in the NS atmosphere. A pair of dashed gray lines shows $10^{7}$ and $10^{5}$ times the Solar abundance of Cd. The red curve indicates the VEM of equation ( 14 ) which is needed to explain the observed flux of the recombination photons. The blue shaded region is allowed by the condition for high ionization [equation ( 18 )]. The magenta curves and shades indicate the constraints by the Thomson optical depth [equation ( 20 )]. The black curve and gray shades indicate the constraints by the self-absorption [equation ( 22 )], respectively.
figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.physical_core: Parameter space diagram of hydrogen number density $n_{\rm H}$ versus cadmium number density $n_x$ in the neutron star atmosphere, delineating the physical viability region defined by volume emission measure (VEM), high ionization requirement, Thomson scattering optical depth, and self-absorption limits requiring an rp-process ash enrichment of $\sim 10^7$ times solar abundance.

analysis.reason: This review directly links young-supernova X-rays to progenitor winds, shock–CSM interaction, and pre-explosion mass-loss history, and it provides scaling relations that can test those hypotheses.
analysis.result: Wind density follows $\rho_w\propto\dot{M}/v_w$. In the Chevalier (1982) model, $\rho_{\mathrm{SN}}=\rho_0(v/v_0)^{-n}(t/t_0)^{-3}$, $\rho_{\mathrm{CSM}}\propto r^{-s}$ with $s=2$ for a steady wind, and $R_{\mathrm{CD}}\propto t^m$ where $m=(n-3)/(n-s)\le1$. For spherical progenitors with $9\le n\le12$, steady-wind thermal $L_x$ falls roughly as $t^{-0.7}$–$t^{-0.8}$ and approaches $t^{-1}$ at larger $n$. The order-of-magnitude luminosity is $L_i=3\times10^{39}g_{ff}C_n(\dot{M}_{-5}/v_{w1})^2(t/10\,\mathrm{d})^{-1}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, with $C_n=1$ for the forward shock and $C_n=(n-3)(n-4)^2/[4(n-2)]$ for the reverse shock; observations constrain $\dot{M}/v_w$. RSG/IIP rates are $\dot{M}\approx10^{-8}$–$10^{-6}\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, while WR Ib/c winds have $v_w\approx1000$–$3000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Many sources show only $1$–$2\,\mathrm{keV}$, below $\sim40\,\mathrm{keV}$ expected for a $\sim5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ forward shock, favoring reverse-shock emission. SN 1993J has early $\dot{M}>10^{-5}\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$; inverse-Compton modeling with $N(E)\propto E^{-p}$ at $p=3$ gives SN 2011ja $(1.2\pm0.2)\times10^{-7}\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$; SN 2011dh is an adiabatic reverse shock with $\dot{M}$ of a few $\times10^{-6}\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. Thermal X-rays are directly proportional to circumstellar density, and a radiative reverse shock can coexist with a non-radiative forward shock.
analysis.reading_entry: 2.1 The Evolution of the CSM Density Profile and Thermal X-ray Luminosity
analysis.problem: The core problem is how X-rays from a young supernova shock expanding in a progenitor wind, rather than pristine ISM, can recover the progenitor mass-loss rate, wind velocity, and CSM density structure despite shock-type and geometry degeneracies.
analysis.method: The analysis uses the Chevalier self-similar shock solution, with ambient density $\rho_{am}=\dot{M}(r_0/r)^s/(4\pi r_0^2 v_w)$, thermal-luminosity scalings for adiabatic and radiative shocks, inverse-Compton spectra $N(E)\propto E^{-p}$, and multiwavelength checks. Radio light curves are fit with Chevalier/Weiler relations to estimate $\dot{M}/v_w$, while optical/IR/UV emission is compared using $L_{\mathrm{opt/IR/UV}}=0.5\,\epsilon\,(\dot{M}/v_w)\,v_{\mathrm{sh}}^3$; X-ray light curves and spectra are preferred because self-similar evolution gives $v\propto t^{m-1}$.
limits: The inferred timing of pre-death wind changes spans hundreds to thousands of years and depends on the adopted wind velocity.
citation_leads: 1 Introduction: “When the SN explodes, the SN shock expands within this wind-blown circumstellar medium”
2.2 Mass Loss Rates Correct to Order of Magnitude: “For SNe evolving in a steady wind, whose luminosity closely follows the $t^{-1}$ decrease”
2.6 Radiative Shocks: “It is possible for the reverse shock to be radiative whereas the forward shock is not”
4 Investigating the Structure and Morphology of the Ambient Medium: “These all point to the existence of a high-density medium close to the star”
7 Discussion: “Thermal X-rays provide the most direct signature of the circumstellar density”
analysis.research_progress: The paper consolidates X-ray diagnostics of progenitor mass loss: steady-wind emission near $L_x\propto t^{-1}$ gives order-of-magnitude $\dot{M}/v_w$ estimates, while departures, shell collisions, and rebrightenings reveal episodic or binary-driven CSM changes. It also distinguishes direct thermal-density constraints from indirect nonthermal and clump-sensitive optical diagnostics.

figures.caption: Figure 8: The interaction of a SN shock wave with an equatorial torus, as may have happened in SN 2014c. The plot shows the density structure from a simulation carried out by the author to study the shock interaction with the equatorial torus in SN 2014c. The VH-1 numerical hydrodynamics code was used Dwarkadas et al. (1996); Dwarkadas and Balick (1998); Dwarkadas (2005); Dwarkadas (2007); Dwarkadas et al. (2010). The impact with the torus drives a transmitted shock into the torus, and a reflected shock back into the ejecta. The shock above and below the torus expands in a lower-density He-rich wind, and therefore, has a much higher velocity. The radio emission arises from this shock. The H $\alpha$ emission arises from the transmitted shock in the torus. The reflected shock and reverse shock in the He-rich wind tend to converge at a point.
figures.label: Fig. 8
figures.physical_core: Two-dimensional hydrodynamic density structure of a supernova shock interacting with an equatorial circumstellar torus (as applicable to SN 2014c), resolving the transmitted shock driven into the dense torus (responsible for H$\alpha$ emission), the high-velocity shock propagating through the low-density He-rich wind (responsible for radio emission), and the convergence of the reflected shock and reverse shock.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The density structure of the medium around SN 1987A in the equatorial plane, using a simulation that combines the photo-ionizing photons from the central pre-SN star with the hydrodynamics of the wind bubble evolution. The inclusion of the stellar photons results in the formation of a dense photo-ionized HII region interior to the shell. Going outwards in radius from the central star, the various regions are (1) the freely expanding wind, (2) the shocked wind, (3) the photo-ionized (HII) region, (4) the dense swept-up shell (equatorial ring) and (5) the red-supergiant wind from the previous epoch. Details of the simulation and the modeling technique are described in Dwarkadas (2022).
figures.label: Fig. 6
figures.physical_core: Equatorial-plane density structure of the circumstellar environment around SN 1987A modeled by coupling pre-supernova stellar photo-ionization with wind bubble hydrodynamics, resolving five distinct radial zones: freely expanding wind, shocked wind, an interior photo-ionized HII region, the dense swept-up equatorial ring shell, and the outer red supergiant wind.

analysis.reason: This statistical afterglow study directly constrains sGRB jet energy and the horizon magnetic field of BNS-merger black holes, which is central to relativistic-jet and compact-remnant engine physics. The reported $E_{\rm k}$, $\eta_\gamma$ and $B_{\rm BH}$ distributions can test whether a Blandford–Znajek engine is viable.
analysis.result: For the 15 strictly constrained (SC) bursts, the median on-axis energy is $\log E_0=52.54$ (68% interval $[51.08,53.43]$), i.e. $E_0\simeq 3.5\times 10^{52}\,\mathrm{erg}$. The beaming-corrected kinetic energy has median $\log E_{\rm k}=49.58$, or $E_{\rm k}\simeq 3.8\times 10^{49}\,\mathrm{erg}$ (68% interval $[5.1\times 10^{48},1.9\times 10^{50}]\,\mathrm{erg}$), and the radiative efficiency has median $\eta_\gamma\simeq 0.35$ (68% interval $[0.09,0.79]$), where $\eta_\gamma=E_\gamma/(E_\gamma+E_{\rm k})$ and $\Gamma_0=300$. Under the BZ scaling $\frac{L_{\rm k}}{1-\eta_\gamma}\approx 10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}\left(\frac{a}{0.9}\right)^2\left(\frac{M_{\rm BH}}{5\,M_\odot}\right)^2\left(\frac{B_{\rm BH}}{10^{16}\,\mathrm{G}}\right)^2$, the SC horizon field is $B_{\rm BH}\simeq 7\times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{G}$ ($7.1^{+15.8}_{-4.8}\times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{G}$ and $7.2^{+16.3}_{-4.9}\times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{G}$ for the two $\tilde\Lambda$ cases), with amplification $\eta_B\equiv B_{\rm BH}/B_{\rm NS}$ of order $10^3$ (medians $1463$ and $1026$). For all 40 bursts the medians shift to $\log(E_0/\mathrm{erg})=52.35$, $\log(E_{\rm k}/\mathrm{erg})=50.20$, $\eta_\gamma=0.26$ and $B_{\rm BH}\sim 2\times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{G}$ ($\log(B_{\rm BH}/\mathrm{G})=16.31$–$16.36$).
analysis.problem: The paper asks what beaming-corrected kinetic energies and gamma-ray efficiencies characterize cosmological short GRBs from BNS mergers, and what black-hole horizon field is required if the Blandford–Znajek process supplies most of the jet energy.
analysis.method: Forty sGRBs with reliable redshifts (Gold Sample, $P_{\rm cc}<0.02$) are fitted burst by burst with an off-axis truncated Gaussian jet in a uniform ISM using afterglowpy, retaining only forward-shock points after removing intervals possibly affected by energy injection, flares, reverse shocks or kilonovae. The angular structure and beam-corrected energy are $E(\theta)=E_0\exp(-\theta^2/2\theta_{\rm c}^2)$ and $E_{\rm k}=E_0\theta_{\rm c}^2\left(1-e^{-\theta_{\rm w}^2/2\theta_{\rm c}^2}\right)$, while $E_{\gamma,\mathrm{iso}}=k\times 4\pi d_{\rm L}^2 f_\gamma/(1+z)$ with a population-mean $k=5$ when the spectrum is unavailable. The 15 SC posteriors supply empirical priors for the other 25 bursts. Jet power is then mapped to the horizon field through $L_{\rm BZ}=\frac{\kappa}{4\pi c}\Omega_{\rm H}^2\Phi_{\rm BH}^2 f(\Omega_{\rm H})$ with $\kappa\sim 0.05$, $\Omega_{\rm H}=ac/(2r_{\rm H})$, $E_{\rm BZ}=E_{\rm k}+E_\gamma$ and $L_{\rm k}\equiv E_{\rm k}/T_{90}$.
assumptions: Magnetic-field constraints assume that a predominantly Blandford–Znajek-powered jet supplies most of the sGRB energy.
Only forward-shock data are fitted, after removal of intervals that may contain additional energy injection or other non-FS components.
limits: The derived horizon fields are conditional on BZ powering and do not exclude magnetar spin-down or neutrino-annihilation engines.
Sparse non-SC afterglows leave $\theta_{\rm c}$, $\theta_{\rm w}$ and $\theta_{\rm obs}$ degenerate, so the full-sample $E_{\rm k}$ and $\eta_\gamma$ distributions differ from the SC results.
An NSBH jet requires tidal disruption of the NS outside the ISCO; most NSBH mergers are argued to contribute little electromagnetic contamination.

analysis.research_progress: Relative to on-axis top-hat inferences, the off-axis Gaussian-jet sample gives a lower beaming-corrected scale $E_{\rm k}\sim 10^{49.6}\,\mathrm{erg}$ and $\eta_\gamma\sim 0.35$ for well-constrained bursts. Matching $E_{\rm BZ}=E_{\rm k}+E_\gamma$ then requires $B_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{15}$–$10^{16}\,\mathrm{G}$ and $\eta_B\sim 10^3$. figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic diagram of an off-axis structured jet. The kinetic energy per unit solid angle $E(\theta)$ decreases with polar angle $\theta$ from the jet axis, with an on-axis value $E_{0}$, a characteristic core angle $\theta_{\mathrm{c}}$, and a truncation angle $\theta_{\mathrm{w}}$. Integrating over solid angle yields the total beaming-corrected kinetic energy $E_{\mathrm{k}}$. An observer located at a viewing angle $\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}$ measures an isotropic-equivalent gamma-ray energy $E_{\gamma,\mathrm{iso}}$, which depends on relativistic beaming and geometric projection effects.

figures.caption: Figure 11: Broadband afterglow fits for the 15 SC GRBs. Red, blue, and green points denote X-ray, optical, and radio observations; triangles mark upper limits. Solid lines show median model light curves generated from hundreds of posterior samples, with shaded regions indicating the 16th–84th percentile uncertainties. Optical and radio fluxes at different bands are converted to those at $5\times 10^{14}$ Hz and $6\times 10^{9}$ Hz, respectively, for visual clarity.

analysis.reason: This is a 3D Monte Carlo radiative-transfer method for He-like K-series lines in photoionized gas around compact objects, including P Cygni profiles seen by XRISM, so it is useful for photoionization and compact-object high-energy spectroscopy but is not a direct FRB, supernova-engine, jet, or neutrino result.
analysis.result: For photoionized Fe at $n=10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ and $\xi=10^{3.1}$, resonance scattering suppresses the cores and boosts the wings of He-like $w$ and $y$ for $N_{\mathrm{H}}\gtrsim10^{22}$ and $\gtrsim10^{23}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, respectively, while $x$ and $z$ stay nearly unchanged. $I/N_{\mathrm{H}}$ declines with column for $w,y$ and is nearly constant for $x,z$; Fe XXV $w,y$ are RS-dominated and form P Cygni profiles in outflow, whereas $x,z$ are mainly RR/II and do not. The $w$ emissivity and Fe$^{+24}$ fraction peak at $\log\xi\simeq 3.3$. A polarized-beam test gives $|Q_{\mathrm{sca}}|/I_{\mathrm{sca}}\simeq 1$ for dipole $w,y$ over most angles, with partial depolarization near $\theta=90^{\circ}$.
analysis.problem: XRISM resolves He-like K-line profiles, including P Cygni profiles, in photoionized plasma around compact objects, but standard 1D radiative transfer uses the escape-probability approximation and does not treat frequency redistribution by resonance scattering explicitly.
analysis.method: SKIRT performs 3D Monte Carlo transfer of He-like K lines ($Z=2$–$30$, $n\to 1$ up to $n=10$) with resonance scattering, radiative recombination, and Li-like inner-shell ionization. The ionization parameter is $\xi\equiv L_{\mathrm{X}}/(n_{\mathrm{H}}r^{2})$, and excited-level populations obey $\dot{\bm{N}}=\bm{\Gamma}\bm{N}+\bm{S}=\bm{0}$ with H-like, He-like, and Li-like densities and $T_{e}$ prescribed externally. Coherent E1 scattering uses $\bm{M}(\theta)=E_1\bm{M}^{(m)}+E_2\bm{M}^{(d)}$ with $E_1+E_2=1$; verification uses $10^{10}$ packets on a Cloudy-structured Fe shell.
assumptions: H-like, He-like, and Li-like densities and the electron temperature are externally prescribed input parameters.
limits: Ionisation balance and electron temperature are not solved self-consistently and are taken as external inputs.

analysis.reason: This is a high-redshift Einstein Probe fast X-ray transient coincident with a classical long GRB, with quantitative afterglow constraints on jet energy, radiative efficiency, and ISM versus wind circumburst medium.
analysis.result: EP250226a/GRB 250226A is at $z=3.314$ with $E_{\mathrm{iso}}\simeq 7.32\times 10^{53}\,\mathrm{erg}$. The X-ray and optical afterglow is nearly achromatic, with no strong rising phase, plateau, or jet break. A uniform-ISM top-hat forward shock is preferred over a wind; the reported fit gives $E_{\mathrm{k,iso}}\simeq 4.07\times 10^{55}\,\mathrm{erg}$, $\eta_{\gamma}\simeq 1.77\%$, and $\log\epsilon_{\mathrm{B,FS}}\simeq -6.52$, so most jet energy remains kinetic. The wind closure estimate $p(\alpha_{\mathrm{o}})\simeq 1.69$ conflicts with $p>2$.

analysis.reason: The paper develops a rigorous scattering-order Stokes recursion and asymptotic eigenmode formalism for polarized transport in Thomson slabs, providing essential theoretical tools to model polarized Comptonization in compact object accretion coronae such as the neutron star X-ray binary 4U 1624–49 observed by IXPE.
analysis.result: In finite Thomson slabs, polarized transport at high scattering orders is dominated by a unique self-adjoint spatial eigenmode with leading eigenvalue $\lambda_0$, yielding an asymptotic escape probability ratio $\lim_{n\to\infty} P_n^\pm / P_{n-1}^\pm = \lambda_0$. In the optically thin limit ($\tau \ll 1$), the leading eigenvalue scales as $\lambda_0 = \frac{3\tau}{4}\left[\ln(1/\tau) + \frac{3}{4} - \gamma_{\rm E} + \mathcal{O}(1/\ln(1/\tau))\right]$ with asymptotic escape polarization approaching $\Pi_\infty^\pm \to -1$. In the optically thick limit ($\tau \gg 1$), transport splits into a diffusion branch $\lambda_{\rm D}(k) = 1 - k^2/3 + \mathcal{O}(k^4)$ and a rapidly suppressed polarization branch $\lambda_{\rm P}(k) = 7/10 - (29/210)k^2 + \mathcal{O}(k^4)$, leading to $\lambda_0 = 1 - k_1^2/3 + \mathcal{O}(k_1^4)$ with wavenumber $k_1 \simeq \pi / (\tau + 2z_0)$ and Milne extrapolation length $z_0 \simeq 0.7121$. The mean scattering order satisfies $\langle N\rangle_{\rm int}^{\rm pol} \simeq \frac{\tau^2}{4} + \frac{3}{2}z_0 \tau$. Application to IXPE/NuSTAR/NICER spectro-polarimetry of 4U 1624–49 constrains electron temperature $kT_{\rm e} \simeq 2.65\text{ keV}$, optical depth $\tau = 13.10^{+1.14}_{-0.98}$, and inclination $i = 81.6^{\circ+2.8}_{-5.6}$, explaining the observed $\sim 3.2\%$ polarization via a slab corona geometry.
analysis.problem: Accurately modeling line-polarized radiation transport, polarization feedback on angular redistribution, escape statistics, and energy-resolved Stokes spectra in finite-optical-depth Thomson scattering coronae around compact objects.
analysis.method: Formulation of an exact scattering-order-resolved Stokes recursion $\bm{\Psi}_{n+1}(t',\mu') = \int_0^\tau {\rm d}t \int_{-1}^1 {\rm d}\mu\, \textbf{P}(\mu',\mu) G(t',t;\mu) \bm{\Psi}_n(t,\mu)$ via a two-coefficient angular closure $(a_n(t), b_n(t))$; spectral decomposition of the self-adjoint integral operator $\textbf{K}_{\rm pol}$ across thin (Galerkin approximation) and thick (half-space Milne matching) limits; synthesis of energy-resolved spectra using the Jones angle-averaged thermal Compton redistribution kernel $\mathcal{R}_{\rm J}$; and cross-validation via an independent polarized Monte Carlo radiative transfer (MCRT) code.

analysis.reason: This work establishes a Self-Organizing Map (SOM) pipeline to classify and inspect emission mechanisms across $36{,}904$ Chandra ACIS X-ray detections, providing useful methodology for compact object high-energy source classification and jet knot diagnostics.
analysis.result: The SOM successfully segregates distinct high-energy radiation regimes: neoAGNs populate the central region with hard spectra and multi-component emission; neoYSOs map to the lower boundary with $kT \in [0.5, 1.5]\ \mathrm{keV}$ and $\Gamma \in [0, 3]$; Binaries cluster in the upper-right with hard spectra ($kT \in [1, 5]\ \mathrm{keV}$) and high variability. In PartOfG sources, it isolates M87 relativistic jet knots (accounting for $\sim 76\%$ of detections at neuron $(x=36, y=9)$) dominated by non-thermal synchrotron emission. SOMClassifier attains Macro-$F_1 = 0.654$ and Micro-$F_1 = 0.737$, classifying $6{,}225$ of $11{,}712$ unlabeled detections ($53\%$ coverage).
analysis.problem: Simple absorbed blackbody ($kT$) and absorbed power-law ($F_E \propto E^{-\nu}$) spectral models yield $\chi_\nu^2 \gg 1$ for high-$\mathrm{S/N}$ Chandra detections, failing to capture diverse physical emission mechanisms across compact binaries, AGNs, and relativistic jet knots in high-dimensional parameter spaces.
analysis.method: Constructs an 11-dimensional feature space from distance-independent hardness ratios $\mathrm{HR}_{xy} = \frac{F(x)-F(y)}{F(x)+F(y)}$, spectral fit parameters ($kT$, $\Gamma$), and multi-band variability metrics ($\mathrm{var\_ratio} = \sigma_{\mathrm{var}} / \mu_{\mathrm{var}}$, $\mathrm{var\_prob}$). Trains a $40 \times 40$ hexagonal SOM using weight update $W(t+1) = W(t) + \theta(t)\cdot\alpha(t)\cdot(V - W(t))$ reaching quantization error $E_q = 0.164$ and topographic error $E_t = 0.037$, and develops an RBF-kernel neighborhood classifier with class weights $w_k = [c / (\mathrm{class\_counts}_k + \varepsilon)]^\gamma$ ($\gamma = 0.7$, $\sigma_f = 0.05$).
limits: The linear dimensionality of the feature space exceeds two (PC1 and PC2 explain $81.4\%$ variance), so a $2\mathrm{D}$ SOM cannot preserve the full 11-dimensional topology.
Simple spectral fits fail for high-$\mathrm{S/N}$ sources ($\chi_\nu^2 \gg 1$), and serendipitous Chandra observations introduce livetime and flux selection biases.

analysis.reason: Paper directly simulates simultaneous BZ jet and BP wind launching from thin accretion disks using resistive GRMHD, yielding quantitative power ratios, geometries and efficiencies relevant to relativistic outflows around compact objects.
analysis.result: All simulations form jets and winds; jets parabolic with $x \propto z^{\mathcal{K}}$ ($\mathcal{K}\approx0.52-0.64$); $\phi\lesssim15$; $P^{\rm BZ}/\dot{M}\approx0.49$ for $a_*=-0.9375$; $P^{\rm BP}/P^{\rm BZ}\approx30\%-35\%$ (constant with $\beta$), rising to $\approx99.5\%$ at $a_*=0.5$; high-$\sigma$ wind reaches $\Gamma_\infty\approx25$ but lacks mass loading; SANE/MAD states distinguished by $\sigma_\Phi/\bar{\Phi}$.
analysis.problem: Ideal GRMHD cannot sustain large-scale poloidal field needed for BP disk winds while launching BZ jets; question is whether resistive thin-disk GRMHD permits simultaneous, observationally consistent jet+wind launching.
analysis.method: Resistive GRMHD in BHAC on Kerr-Schild coordinates with $\eta(r,\theta)=0.50pt\,c_s\exp[-2(r\cos\theta/100pt)^2]$, cooling $L=\xi\Omega_K p/(\hat\gamma-1)(Y-1+|Y-1|)$, initial $\beta=1-10$, $H/R=0.05-0.1$, $a_*=\pm0.9375,0.5$; MAD parameter $\phi=\Phi/\sqrt{\dot{M}}$; outflow classification by outermost horizon-anchored field line and $Be>0$; power decomposed into EM/PAKE/EN components.

analysis.reason: Investigates whether non-axisymmetric $w$-mode instabilities deplete the rotational energy reservoir of strangeon ergostars as alternative sGRB central engines, finding them dynamically stable along maximum-energy-extraction paths.
analysis.result: Along maximum-energy-extraction paths across all 12 Lennard-Jones strangeon EOS models (A–L), both the $l=m=2$ axial-led and polar-led $w$-modes remain strictly damped with $\mathrm{Im}(\sigma) > 0$. The stability margin $\eta_{\Omega} = \Omega_1 / \Omega_{\rm crit} < 1$ demonstrates that even for the most weakly damped configuration (Model H), the critical rotation rate exceeds the extraction-path rate by $\approx 8\%$ (i.e. $\Omega_{\rm crit} \approx 1.08\,\Omega_1$), confirming that the rotational energy reservoir of $\sim 0.01\,M_\odot c^2 \sim 10^{52}\,\mathrm{erg}$ is preserved against gravitational radiation.
analysis.problem: Whether non-axisymmetric $w$-mode instability in rapidly rotating strangeon ergostars operates as a competitive dissipation channel that siphons rotational energy into gravitational waves instead of powering relativistic jets in short gamma-ray bursts.
analysis.method: Linearized Einstein-fluid perturbation theory in the Hilbert gauge $\nabla^a \psi_{ab} = 0$, discretized into a quadratic matrix eigenvalue problem $(\mathbf{A}_0 + \sigma\mathbf{A}_1 + \sigma^2\mathbf{A}_2)\boldsymbol{x} = 0$ via Chebyshev pseudo-spectral expansion, combined with exterior complex scaling (ECS) for outgoing waves and explicit surface jump matching $\left.(\partial_r \psi_{ab}^{\rm in} - \partial_r \psi_{ab}^{\rm out})\right|_\Sigma = \frac{16\pi \rho_{\rm sur} \xi}{W_\Sigma} u_a u_b$.
assumptions: Strangeon stars are described by phenomenological Lennard-Jones quark matter EOS with finite surface density \rho_{\rm sur} \neq 0.

IV.1 $w$-mode stability along maximum-energy-extraction paths: “we calculate the complex eigenvalues of the axial-led and polar-led $w$-mode branches.”
V Conclusions: “these modes therefore do not develop the instability-driven growth”
Stellar-surface matching.: “a self-bound stellar surface contributes explicitly to the matching of the metric derivatives.”

analysis.reason: The paper targets the ANITA-IV upward air-shower versus IceCube null ultra-high-energy neutrino tension, so it is relevant to high-energy neutrino observations, but its dark-sector mass flip-flop is peripheral to FRB, supernova-engine, and jet studies.
analysis.result: Four near-horizon ANITA-IV upward showers are attributed to atmospheric $N_2\to N_1 Z'$ rather than $\nu_\tau$. Matter-induced ordering reversal opens underground $N_1\to N_2 Z'$ while kinematics $|M_1(h)-M_2|\le M_{Z'}$ blocks decays at IceCube. For $M_{Z'}=1\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and $y_1=-1$, BP1 and BP2 give $(h_-,h_+)\simeq(-1.15,14.77)\,\mathrm{km}$ and $(-0.96,9.95)\,\mathrm{km}$. At $g_{12}=10^{-5}$, $\int\mathcal{A}\,d\mathcal{H}=1.7\,\mathrm{km}^{2}\,\mathrm{sr}$ (BP1) and $5.4\,\mathrm{km}^{2}\,\mathrm{sr}$ (BP2); at $E_1=20\,\mathrm{EeV}$, increasing $g_{12}$ to $10^{-4}$ raises the BP1 peak from $10$ to $26\,\mathrm{km}^{2}$. The lab lengths scale as $\ell_i\simeq E_i/[M_i\Gamma_{ij}]$ and $\ell_{Z'}\propto E_{Z'}g_B^{-2}$; for $g_B=10^{-3}$, $E_{Z'}=1\,\mathrm{EeV}$ and $M_{Z'}\gtrsim 0.7\,\mathrm{GeV}$, $\ell_{Z'}<0.1\,\mathrm{km}$. Normalized to four ANITA-IV events, the associated IceCube signal is $\ll 1$, while PUEO's first flight expects about 3 events. The standard $\nu_\tau$ joint tension exceeds $7\sigma$, and a rare-transient case still exceeds $5\sigma$.

analysis.problem: ANITA-IV reports four upward-going, non-inverted, cosmic-ray-like air showers just below the horizon, nominally consistent with ultra-high-energy $\nu_\tau$, but IceCube sees no corresponding events, creating a $>7\sigma$ tension ($>5\sigma$ even for rare transients).
analysis.method: Two dark fermions $N_1,N_2$, an ultralight scalar $\phi$, and a GeV-scale $Z'$ undergo a density-dependent mass flip-flop, $M_1(\mathbf{x})=M_1^{(0)}+\delta M_1(\mathbf{x})$. For $M_i>M_j+M_{Z'}$, the rest-frame width is $\Gamma_{ij}$ with $\lambda(a,b,c)=a^2+b^2+c^2-2ab-2ac-2bc$; the lab length is $\ell_i(s,E_i)\simeq E_i/[M_i(s)\Gamma_{ij}(s)]$, and survival follows an exponential integral of $\ell_i^{-1}$. In the unpolarized ultrarelativistic limit, $z\equiv E_{Z'}/E_i$ is uniform on $(z_-,z_+)$. ANITA-IV effective area is computed semi-analytically along $N_1\to N_2\to\mathrm{EAS}$ using position-dependent decay and energy transport, matched to the Standard Model $\nu_\tau$ visible-shower response.
assumptions: $Z'$ hadronic decays with $B_h\simeq 1$ are prompt because their lab lengths are much smaller than atmospheric shower-development scales, so the shower origin is placed at the $N_2$ decay.

analysis.reason: This is a low-latency BNS early-warning search method for third-generation detectors, useful for compact-object multi-messenger follow-up, but it does not directly study FRB/PRS, supernova engines, jets, neutrinos, or circumstellar interaction.
analysis.result: A CNN with $\mathcal{N}=10^{3}$ templates reaches a sensitivity distance comparable to SFT matched filtering, which instead needs approximately $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{7}$ templates, about four orders of magnitude more. For $f_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\min}\in\{2,3,4,5\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the quoted evaluation time falls from minutes to milliseconds, a speed-up of about $1.6\times10^{4}$–$4.0\times10^{4}$; the CNN per-template cost is $\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle\approx(3$–$25)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. At fixed template number, sensitivity follows $\langle s\rangle\sim\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}(1-\langle\mu\rangle)$ with $\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}\propto\int_{f_{\min}}^{10\,\mathrm{Hz}}f^{-7/3}/S_n(f)\,df$.
analysis.problem: Early warning of binary neutron-star inspirals in third-generation detectors is limited by the computing cost of evaluating the detection statistic at low latency.
analysis.method: Early inspirals are represented by narrowband SFTs with $T_{\mathrm{SFT}}=31\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta k=51$ bins about $f(t;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}})=f_{\max}[1+(256/5)(\pi f_{\max})^{8/3}(G\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}/c^{3})^{5/3}(t_{\max}-t)]^{-3/8}$. A CNN minimizes binary cross-entropy and searches only $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}$, while the SFT statistic $\mathcal{X}$ is maximized analytically over phase and luminosity distance and then over an eight-dimensional bank. Latency is modeled as $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{N}\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle$, with $f_s=40\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for the 3, 4, and 5 Hz regimes.
limits: For lower chirp masses, evolution from $f_{\min}$ to $f_{\max}$ can exceed the fixed analysis window, so the signal is aligned at $f_{\max}$ and only its late portion is retained.

analysis.reason: This ZTF spectroscopic census of hydrogen-rich SLSNe directly constrains circumstellar interaction, pre-explosion mass loss, and possible Ia-CSM contamination, which are central to supernova-engine and CSM studies.
analysis.result: Of 106 hydrogen-rich SLSNe, 105 show narrow Balmer emission and are spectroscopically SLSNe-IIn; SN 2022lvm is the sole broad-lined SLSN-II in the discussed 2021–2022 subset comparison (1/36, 2.8%). Measured $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ spans $2.2\times10^{40}$ to $1.5\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ (median $2.6\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$). The median Balmer decrement rises from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterward, below the Ia-CSM comparison medians 6.58 and 17.76. After excluding the SLSN-II and six Ia-CSM-like objects, median shell speed correlates with peak magnitude ($r=0.63$, $p=0.010$): brighter events tend to have lower $v_{\rm s}$. For 13 calibrated objects at $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon=0.5$, $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ from $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Six of 105 narrow-line events ($\sim6\%$) are Ia-CSM-like. Narrow interaction lines can persist beyond $+200$ d, with no Balmer morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn relative to fainter SNe IIn.
analysis.problem: Whether luminous narrow-line SLSNe-IIn are spectroscopically only the bright extreme of SNe IIn, what dense hydrogen-rich CSM and enhanced pre-explosion mass loss they require, and whether narrow Balmer lines plus high luminosity uniquely imply core collapse rather than Ia-CSM.
analysis.method: The study uses 304 optical spectra of 106 ZTF events selected at rest-frame peak $M\leq-19.9$ mag, with phases $(t-t_{\rm peak})/(1+z)$ and fluxes scaled by $10^{-0.4(m_{\rm GP}-m_{\rm syn})}$ from Gaussian-process light curves (287 absolutely calibrated). Balmer luminosity, pEW and FWHM are measured after local continuum subtraction. Single-epoch Monte Carlo electron-scattering snapshots (escatter; $10^{5}$ H$\alpha$ photons outside a cold dense shell) fit line profiles. Mass-loss rates use $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}\frac{v_{\rm s}^{3}}{u_{\rm w}}$ and $\dot{M}=\frac{2L}{\epsilon}\frac{u_{\rm w}}{v_{\rm s}^{3}}$, with luminosity integrated from the spectra and a blackbody extension to 3000–20000 Å.

analysis.result: Stochastic acceleration appreciably changes the downstream particle spectrum whenever $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$. analysis.result: Homogeneous collective precession (HCP) is a rotating-frame fixed point, but it is not always attracting. For $0.034\le\kappa_e\le0.060$, successive maxima of $P_z$ period-double eight times toward a stable $256$-cycle, with spacing ratios approaching $\delta_{\rm F}\simeq4.669$. At $\kappa_e=0.055025$ the leading Lyapunov estimate is $\widehat\lambda_1\simeq2.8\times10^{-3}$ for bounded irregular evolution. analysis.result: A CNN with $\mathcal{N}=10^{3}$ templates reaches a sensitivity distance comparable to SFT matched filtering, which instead needs approximately $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{7}$ templates, about four orders of magnitude more. For $f_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\min}\in\{2,3,4,5\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the quoted evaluation time falls from minutes to milliseconds, a speed-up of about $1.6\times10^{4}$–$4.0\times10^{4}$; the CNN per-template cost is $\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle\approx(3$–$25)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. At fixed template number, sensitivity follows $\langle s\rangle\sim\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}(1-\langle\mu\rangle)$ with $\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}\propto\int_{f_{\min}}^{10\,\mathrm{Hz}}f^{-7/3}/S_n(f)\,df$.
analysis.problem: Early warning of binary neutron-star inspirals in third-generation detectors is limited by the computing cost of evaluating the detection statistic at low latency.
analysis.method: Early inspirals are represented by narrowband SFTs with $T_{\mathrm{SFT}}=31\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta k=51$ bins about $f(t;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}})=f_{\max}[1+(256/5)(\pi f_{\max})^{8/3}(G\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}/c^{3})^{5/3}(t_{\max}-t)]^{-3/8}$. A CNN minimizes binary cross-entropy and searches only $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}$, while the SFT statistic $\mathcal{X}$ is maximized analytically over phase and luminosity distance and then over an eight-dimensional bank. Latency is modeled as $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{N}\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle$, with $f_s=40\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for the 3, 4, and 5 Hz regimes.
limits: For lower chirp masses, evolution from $f_{\min}$ to $f_{\max}$ can exceed the fixed analysis window, so the signal is aligned at $f_{\max}$ and only its late portion is retained.

analysis.reason: This ZTF spectroscopic census of hydrogen-rich SLSNe directly constrains circumstellar interaction, pre-explosion mass loss, and possible Ia-CSM contamination, which are central to supernova-engine and CSM studies.
analysis.result: Of 106 hydrogen-rich SLSNe, 105 show narrow Balmer emission and are spectroscopically SLSNe-IIn; SN 2022lvm is the sole broad-lined SLSN-II in the discussed 2021–2022 subset comparison (1/36, 2.8%). Measured $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ spans $2.2\times10^{40}$ to $1.5\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ (median $2.6\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$). The median Balmer decrement rises from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterward, below the Ia-CSM comparison medians 6.58 and 17.76. After excluding the SLSN-II and six Ia-CSM-like objects, median shell speed correlates with peak magnitude ($r=0.63$, $p=0.010$): brighter events tend to have lower $v_{\rm s}$. For 13 calibrated objects at $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon=0.5$, $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ from $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Six of 105 narrow-line events ($\sim6\%$) are Ia-CSM-like. Narrow interaction lines can persist beyond $+200$ d, with no Balmer morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn relative to fainter SNe IIn.
analysis.problem: Whether luminous narrow-line SLSNe-IIn are spectroscopically only the bright extreme of SNe IIn, what dense hydrogen-rich CSM and enhanced pre-explosion mass loss they require, and whether narrow Balmer lines plus high luminosity uniquely imply core collapse rather than Ia-CSM.
analysis.method: The study uses 304 optical spectra of 106 ZTF events selected at rest-frame peak $M\leq-19.9$ mag, with phases $(t-t_{\rm peak})/(1+z)$ and fluxes scaled by $10^{-0.4(m_{\rm GP}-m_{\rm syn})}$ from Gaussian-process light curves (287 absolutely calibrated). Balmer luminosity, pEW and FWHM are measured after local continuum subtraction. Single-epoch Monte Carlo electron-scattering snapshots (escatter; $10^{5}$ H$\alpha$ photons outside a cold dense shell) fit line profiles. Mass-loss rates use $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}\frac{v_{\rm s}^{3}}{u_{\rm w}}$ and $\dot{M}=\frac{2L}{\epsilon}\frac{u_{\rm w}}{v_{\rm s}^{3}}$, with luminosity integrated from the spectra and a blackbody extension to 3000–20000 Å.
assumptions: Quoted mass-loss rates use the adopted CSM-interaction model with $\epsilon=0.5$ and $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, commonly with a shock speed of $5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
limits: Inferred mass-loss rates are order-of-magnitude estimates rather than precise progenitor mass-loss histories.

analysis.problem: The work asks which progenitor mass is allowed by the nebular spectra of SN 1987A and whether the post-500 d optical deficit and UV behavior come from $\gamma$-ray leakage, molecular cooling, newly formed internal dust, or background-star contamination, rather than from circumstellar interaction.
analysis.method: One-dimensional, time-dependent NLTE radiative transfer with CMFGEN uses shuffled-shell macroscopic mixing and no microscopic mixing. Molecules are omitted in the global solution; a CO test retains only 10% of the C/O-shell absorbed decay power. After $\sim500\,\mathrm{d}$, $0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ silicate dust is added only inside the metal-rich region at $v<2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Spectra are placed at $D=49.59\,\mathrm{kpc}$ with $E(B-V)=0.15\,\mathrm{mag}$, and model comparisons are normalized by absorbed decay power.
assumptions: The $^{56}$Ni decay chain dominates the radioactive power at all modeled epochs, and $^{56}$Ni bubbles and CSM interaction are omitted.

The density evolution of the perturbed cases is displayed in the top two rows, while density slices along the x-axis for all three cases are shown in the bottom row. The first row shows the plus perturbation propagating toward the center of the star and eventually collapsing to a black hole, with the apparent horizon visible at time 512M, indicated by the black circle in the top panels and the blue vertical line in the bottom panels. The second row shows the minus perturbation also reaching the center, where it reflects and subsequently triggers the dispersal of most of the radiation.

analysis.reason: This radiative Kerr-magnetosphere GRPIC study is useful for relativistic-jet launching and compact-object VHE emission because it quantifies current closure and gamma-ray output relative to the Blandford–Znajek power, but it is peripheral to FRB, pulsar-wind, and supernova-engine problems.
analysis.result: A polar spark gap and a variable equatorial current sheet jointly sustain the global poloidal current. With low pair multiplicity, synchrotron–curvature (SC) cooling leaves the overall structure largely unchanged but drives spark-gap electric-field oscillations; polar and equatorial variability have no significant cross-correlation and $\Delta t\sim l_{\rm rec}/(\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}c)\sim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$ at $\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}\sim +0.1$. Post-processed bolometric luminosities are $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ (reported in the opening summary as SC up to $\sim 1\%$ and inverse Compton $\sim 0.1\%$ of the BZ luminosity), with spark-gap photons reaching sub-TeV energies. Balancing $t_{\rm SC}=6\pi m_{\rm e}c/(\sigma_{\rm T}f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}B_{0}^{2}\Gamma)$ and $t_{\rm acc}\approx\Gamma m_{\rm e}c/(ef_{D}B_{0})$ gives $\Gamma_{\rm max}=\sqrt{f_{D}/f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}}\,\Gamma_{\rm SC}\simeq 3.7\times 10^{6}$ for representative equatorial $B_{0}\sim 10^{2}\,\mathrm{G}$.
analysis.problem: The paper investigates how a polar spark gap and an equatorial current sheet jointly close the global poloidal current in a radiative, charge-starved Kerr black-hole magnetosphere, and how SC cooling changes particle acceleration, variability, and gamma-ray signatures relative to observed VHE flares.
analysis.method: The study uses axisymmetric 2D GRPIC in Kerr–Schild 3+1 form, evolving $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{B}=-\nabla\times\bm{E}$ and $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{D}=\nabla\times\bm{H}-\frac{4\pi}{c}\bm{J}$ with Hamiltonian particles, ambient-photon inverse Compton scattering, and two-photon pair creation. It compares no cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=\infty$, with marginal slow cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=800$, from a Wald vertical field at $a=0.99$, $\tilde{B}_{0}=5\times 10^{3}$, $\varepsilon_{0}=5\times 10^{-2}$, and $\tau_{0}=10$ ($\sigma_{0}\simeq 1.2\times 10^{4}$), followed by ray tracing. The SC drag is $\bm{g}\simeq-\frac{2}{3}\frac{e^{4}}{m_{\rm e}^{2}c^{4}}\Gamma^{2}\bm{\beta}B_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}$.
assumptions: The adopted plasma supply has a low pair multiplicity, explicitly described as a low-pair-multiplicity parameter choice.
limits: Synthetic luminosity-variation amplitudes are smaller than the order-of-magnitude enhancements in prominent VHE flares.

analysis.research_progress: At low multiplicity, radiative cooling is an incremental correction to force-free current closure: the parabolic near-horizon geometry and global circuit persist, while pair-production efficiency causes gap oscillations. Both regions vary on $\Delta t\lesssim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$, but only the polar region shows a distinct oscillation peak and their cross-correlation is insignificant. The radiative yields satisfy $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$, with slow- and fast-cooling spectra $\Gamma dN/d\Gamma\propto\Gamma^{0}$ and $\propto\Gamma^{-1}$.

Solid (dashed) curves denote the msCl (nCl) model; blue (orange) curves represent electrons (positrons). ( 12 ), with $(f_{D},f_{B_{\perp,\rm eff}})=(10^{-1},10^{-1})$ for (a) and $(10^{-1},1.0)$ for (d)), and the time- and volume-averaged magnetization, $\sigma_{\pm}=B^{2}/4\pi n_{\pm}m_{\rm e}c^{2}$, respectively.
figures.label: Fig. 7

analysis.reason: The paper quantifies when downstream second-order Fermi acceleration at SNR shocks can reshape cosmic-ray spectra and the associated pp gamma-ray flux, which is useful for supernova-shock and high-energy studies, but it does not treat central engines, shock breakout, FRBs, or jets.
analysis.result: Stochastic acceleration appreciably changes the downstream particle spectrum whenever $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$. For standard Model I parameters, including stochastic acceleration and wave feedback increases the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ and $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ by $\sim 50\%$. For an undamped $f(p)\propto p^{-4}$ Kolmogorov cascade, $P t_{\rm age}/P_{\rm CR}\approx (3/4)\eta/\xi_{\rm CR}$; acceleration times scale as $\tau_{\rm acc}\sim p^{1/3}$ (Kolmogorov) or $\sim p^{1/2}$ (Kraichnan), while source-free inertial spectra are $W\sim k^{-5/3}$ and $W\sim k^{-3/2}$. Upstream self-generated waves alone do not significantly modify the downstream spectrum because the cascade rapidly removes their energy.
analysis.reading_entry: Evolution of Turbulence and Stochastic Acceleration Downstream
analysis.problem: The paper asks whether particles accelerated at an SNR shock and then advected downstream have their spectrum modified by second-order Fermi acceleration, and whether that change appears in $pp\to\pi^0$ gamma rays, despite strong-shock DSA spectra being nearly universal for $M_s\gg 1$.
analysis.method: The particle distribution and turbulent spectrum are evolved together through $\partial_t f=p^{-2}\partial_p(p^2 D_{pp}\partial_p f)$ and $\partial_t W+\partial_k F=-\Gamma W+S-D$, using quasi-linear $D_{pp}$, resonant damping $\Gamma$, and Kolmogorov or Kraichnan cascades. The SNR downstream is split into independent shells with adiabatic losses, and the $pp$ gamma-ray flux is integrated with Naima and Kafexhiu cross sections, comparing cases with and without stochastic acceleration and wave feedback.
citation_leads: Evolution of Turbulence and Stochastic Acceleration Downstream: “stochastic acceleration to be important whenever $\eta\gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$, changing appreciably the particle spectrum.”
Conclusions: “the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ -- 100 GeV increases by $\sim 50\%$ when stochastic acceleration and wave feedback are taken into account.”
analysis.research_progress: Beyond shock-only DSA, the calculation identifies $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$ as the regime where downstream stochastic acceleration matters and finds a $\sim 50\%$ rise in the $1$--$100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ flux for Model I. Significant modification requires the cascade, wave damping, and a downstream turbulence source to be retained together.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Wave energy spectra (left panel) and accelerated particle spectra (right panel) downstream of a type II SNR, with parameters $\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$ and Kraichnan turbulent cascading. Colors indicate fluid parcels that crossed the shock and entered the downstream region at different moments along the SNR’s lifetime, $t_{0}=10$ yr (blue liens), 100 yr (orange lines) and 750 yr (green lines). These spectra evolve from each $t_{0}$ (dashed lines) until the SNR’s age $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr (solid lines).
figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.physical_core: Downstream of a type II SNR ($\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$, Kraichnan cascade), fluid parcels that crossed the shock at $t_0=10$, $100$, and $750$ yr evolve from their injection spectra (dashed) to $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr (solid). Wave energy $W(k)$ and the particle distribution $f(p)$ change together because resonant damping by the particles is nonlinearly coupled to the turbulence that drives second-order Fermi acceleration.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Hadronic gamma-ray fluxes at $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr from the downstream of a type II SNR with parameters $\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$ and Kraichnan turbulent cascading (same as Figure 3 ), assuming a distance of $d=1$ kpc to us. Fluxes without the effects of stochastic acceleration are shown as dashed lines. The total flux (blue lines) is the sum of the fluxes coming from regions that crossed the shock at all times $t_{0}$ throughout the lifetime of the SNR, which we divide into $0<t_{0}<100$ yr (yellow lines), $100$ yr $<t_{0}<500$ yr (green lines) and $500$ yr $<t_{0}<t_{\rm age}$ (red lines).
figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.physical_core: Hadronic $\gamma$-ray flux at $d=1$ kpc and $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr from $pp$ scattering in the same downstream. Solid curves include stochastic acceleration; dashed curves do not. The total (blue) is split by shock-crossing epoch: $0<t_0<100$ yr, $100<t_0<500$ yr, and $500\,{\rm yr}<t_0<t_{\rm age}$, so the spectral change is tied to how long each parcel spends in the turbulent downstream.

analysis.reason: The paper is relevant to supernova and compact-merger neutrino transport because collisional flavor conversion need not settle to an attracting fixed point, and the resulting cycles or chaos shift time-averaged flavor populations. It is worth knowing rather than essential because it is a specialized kinetic bifurcation study, not a direct engine or high-energy observational constraint.
analysis.result: Homogeneous collective precession (HCP) is a rotating-frame fixed point, but it is not always attracting. As the electron collision rate $\kappa_e$ approaches $0.0025$ from below, the target growth rate and the HCP number offset vanish together (supercritical Hopf); near $\kappa_e\simeq0.018$ a finite-amplitude pair appears, and the unstable branch merges with the target near $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221$ (subcritical Hopf). An independent HCP crossing occurs at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0200194578$, before target destabilization at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221481171$. For $0.034\le\kappa_e\le0.060$, successive maxima of $P_z$ period-double eight times toward a stable $256$-cycle, with spacing ratios approaching $\delta_{\rm F}\simeq4.669$. At $\kappa_e=0.055025$ the leading Lyapunov estimate is $\widehat\lambda_1\simeq2.8\times10^{-3}$ for bounded irregular evolution. The HCP balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, while averages obey $s[\langle u\rangle_T^2+\mathrm{Var}_T(u)]=\langle z\rangle_T\langle Z\rangle_T+\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)-\tfrac12\mathcal{B}_{u^2}$. The largest reported HCP-versus-time-average population deviation is $8.03\%$, set by the mean coherent torque rather than by stationarity.
analysis.problem: The issue is whether a collisionally balanced HCP state attracts neutrino flavor trajectories or whether collisional flavor instability instead produces Hopf cycles, period doubling, and chaos, and how far HCP or mean-only estimates miss the time-averaged flavor populations.
analysis.method: The full quantum kinetic equations are linearized in the rotating frame, including the response of the self-interaction field; after removal of the common phase, local attraction requires all seven Jacobian eigenvalues to have negative real parts. For energy-independent rates the collective matrix follows the monochromatic kinetics and residuals contract at least as $e^{-\kappa_* t}$. Root number is fixed by the sign of $\mathcal{C}$, and $\kappa_e$ is scanned with multiple shooting and Lyapunov estimates. Steady balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, whereas the time-averaged identity keeps $\mathrm{Var}_T(u)$ and $\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)$.
assumptions: Existence of an HCP state does not imply attraction; attraction is judged by linearizing the full quantum kinetic equations in the rotating frame, including self-interaction response.
limits: Because of fluctuation and coherent-torque terms, an HCP estimate need not equal the time average; the maximum reported deviation is $8.03\%$, and relative spectral errors also depend on $c_E$.

analysis.reason: The paper establishes an intrinsic hard X-ray point-source excess in the Nuclear Stellar Disk and associates it with high-mass white-dwarf intermediate polars and possibly millisecond pulsars, which is relevant compact-object high-energy context but not central to FRB, jet, neutrino, or supernova-engine studies.
analysis.result: Within the NSD ($|l|\lesssim 1.3^{\circ}$, $|b|\lesssim 0.3^{\circ}$), XMM-Newton finds a concentration of intrinsically hard point sources. Plane sources are softer, with mean $\mathrm{HR}\simeq 0.1$ (PN) and $\simeq-0.3$ (MOS), where $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$, $H=4.5$–$12\,\mathrm{keV}$, and $S=2.0$–$4.5\,\mathrm{keV}$. Inside-versus-outside HR distributions differ at $>8\sigma$. At $-1.05^{\circ}<l<0.55^{\circ}$, observed $\mathrm{HR}\gtrsim 0.3$ exceeds $\mathrm{HR}<0.2$ predicted for $5\times10^{22}<N_{\rm H}<8\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Hard and soft longitude/latitude distributions differ at $>12\sigma/9\sigma$ ($p=2\times10^{-35}/3\times10^{-20}$). Scale heights are $h_{l,\rm s}=2^{\circ}$ ($\sim280\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{b,\rm s}=0.31^{\circ}$ ($\sim44\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{l,\rm h}=0.66^{\circ}$ ($\sim90\,\mathrm{pc}$), and $h_{b,\rm h}=0.17^{\circ}$ ($\sim24\,\mathrm{pc}$). The stellar-mass distribution follows the soft sources better than the hard sources. The hard NSD population most likely consists of intermediate polars with high $M_{\rm WD}$, possibly plus MSPs; representative partial covering at $kT=36\,\mathrm{keV}$ gives $\mathrm{HR}\sim0.82$ versus $\sim0.36$ without it, and $\langle kT\rangle\approx34\,\mathrm{keV}$ for IPs versus $\approx11\,\mathrm{keV}$ for polars. The $\log N$–$\log S$ slope is $\alpha\sim1.35$–$1.5$.
analysis.problem: The paper tests whether the hard X-ray point-source concentration overlapping the NSD is an intrinsically harder compact-object population or only an artifact of large line-of-sight $N_{\rm H}$, and what that population implies for the unresolved sources underlying the Galactic-center and Galactic-ridge X-ray emission.
analysis.method: Using the XMM-Newton Heritage Survey and cleaned 4XMM-DR14 sources over $|l|<10^{\circ}$, $|b|<1^{\circ}$, the authors compare $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$ inside and outside the NSD with count-rate and exposure-matched K–S tests. Because most sources lack reliable spectra, they simulate 274 parameter sets with XSPEC fakeit and EPIC-PN responses: $\mathrm{tbabs}\times\mathrm{powerlaw}$ for $\Gamma=0$–$3$ and absorbed APEC for $kT=1$–$36\,\mathrm{keV}$, spanning $N_{\rm H}=(1$–$30)\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and $Z_{\rm Fe}=(0.5,1,2)Z_{\odot}$.

analysis.reason: IXPE polarization and spectral constraints on the Cyg X-1 corona’s aspect ratio and axial outflow are relevant to compact-object high-energy observations and jet-aligned geometry, but the work is peripheral to FRB, supernova-engine, and shock-breakout studies.
analysis.result: IXPE measures a 2–8 keV polarization of $(4.01\pm 0.20)\%$ parallel to the radio jet at inclination $27.51^\circ$, whereas static corona models give only $1$–$2.5\%$. Cylindrical outflow models with $h=H/(2R)\leq 0.8$ and $\beta_{\rm top}=0.5$–$0.9$ simultaneously give $\Gamma=1.6$ and $\sim 4\%$ polarization parallel to the symmetry axis; larger $h$ has $q_{\rm max}<4\%$ even at $\beta_{\rm top}=0.99$. Outflow suppresses radiative feedback as $f_\beta\propto(1-\beta)^2$. The discussion gives $\delta\approx 1.56$, $L\approx 0.3L_{\rm iso}$, $\ell=35.4(L_{\rm iso}/0.5\%L_{\rm Edd})(r_g/R)$, $t_{\rm IC}=0.03(R/r_g)R/c$, $B_{\rm eq}\approx 1.1\times 10^{7}(R/r_g)^{-1}\,\mathrm{G}$, $\sigma\approx 6.9(R/r_g)^{-1}$ and $v_A\approx 0.9c$, favoring a pair corona. The IXPE polarization-angle difference is $3.3^\circ\pm 3.2^\circ$; requiring the band-to-band Faraday difference to be $<0.11$ rad yields $\eta_\Delta<0.14(B_\parallel/10^{7}\,\mathrm{G})^{-1}$.
analysis.reading_entry: III Results - limits on the corona’s aspect ratio
analysis.problem: Static Comptonizing coronae underpredict the hard-state polarization of Cyg X-1: IXPE finds about $4\%$ polarization parallel to the radio jet, while static models give only $1$–$2.5\%$. The question is how small $h=H/(2R)$ must be and how fast an axial outflow must be to reproduce both $\Gamma=1.6$ and the polarization.
analysis.method: polrad-3D Monte Carlo polarized transfer is run in a three-dimensional cylinder with the symmetry axis along $z$, temporarily neglecting general relativity. Continuity gives $n(z)\propto\beta^{-1}$, with Thomson depths $t_z=\bar{n}\sigma_T H$ and $t_r=\bar{n}\sigma_T R$. Constant-$\beta$ and accelerating profiles from $\beta_0=0.1$ to $\beta_{\rm top}$ are compared for a $100\,\mathrm{keV}$ Maxwell–Jüttner plasma and unpolarized isotropic $10\,\mathrm{eV}$ cyclo-synchrotron seeds, using invariant optical depth and the full Klein–Nishina Fano matrix. Grids in $t_z$ and $\beta_{\rm top}$, with up to $6.4\times 10^8$ photons, are matched to $\Gamma=1.6$ and $q=4\%$ at $i=27.5^\circ$.
assumptions: The radial scale is taken to be $R\sim r_g$ because the flow is unlikely to concentrate the required energy into much smaller regions.
limits: Only $h\leq 0.8$ with $\beta_{\rm top}=0.5$–$0.9$ jointly fits $\Gamma=1.6$ and $4\%$ polarization; larger $h$ remains below $4\%$ even at $\beta_{\rm top}=0.99$.

The dotted lines show results from interpolating the results from the original calculation grid. The solid lines and data points are from the final simulations. All results show models which give $\Gamma=1.6$.
figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.physical_core: Normalized Stokes parameter q=Q/I for coronas that produce photon index Γ=1.6, comparing constant-velocity outflows with plasmas accelerating linearly in depth from β0=0.1 to β_top; positive q means polarization parallel to the symmetry (jet) axis.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The top panel shows the highest polarization $q$ on the $\Gamma=1.6$ contour at a viewing inclination of 27.5 ∘ as a function of the aspect ratio of the corona in the stationary frame for outflows with constant $\beta$ (blue lines), $\beta$ linear in depth (red lines), and linear in height (green lines). For aspect ratios $h\leq 0.8$, we find solutions matching the observed $q=4$ %. The yellow band shows the observed value with a 0.5% systematic uncertainty band. The center and lower panels are only for the velocity stratified coronas. The center panel shows the $\beta_{\rm top}$ required to match the observed $q$ for $h\leq 0.8$, as well as the $\beta_{\rm top}$ -values giving the highest $q$ for h $\geq$ 1.6. The hatched regions show the values entering the yellow band of 4% $\pm$ 0.5%. The right $y$ -axis translates the $\beta_{\rm top}$ -values into the corresponding Lorentz factors. The lower panel shows the vertical (and for $h\geq 0.8$ the radial) depths of the models achieving $q\,=\,$ 4%, or, for models that fail, the depths that give the highest PD while $\Gamma\,=\,1.6$.
figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.physical_core: On the Γ=1.6 contour at inclination 27.5°, maximum q versus stationary-frame aspect ratio h for constant-β and velocity-stratified coronas; only h≤0.8 reaches the observed q≈4%±0.5%, requiring β_top≈0.5–0.9, with the corresponding vertical/radial depths.

The indices are $\gamma=2.76(18{:}15)$ and $\gamma=3.13(57{:}37)$. The three-segment split reaches $3.84\sigma$, and the global significance over eight schemes is $3.43\sigma$. analysis.problem: Earlier full-plane IceCube searches reached about $4.5\sigma$ and $5.7\sigma$ using GeV--TeV gamma-ray templates. The question is how the neutrino normalization and spectral index vary with Galactic longitude without assuming an emission model, and whether that spectrum matches hadronic gamma-ray data.
analysis.method: A multi-component unbinned likelihood uses cascades and, in each segment, a spatially uniform power law $\Phi_k(E_\nu)=\Phi_{0,k}E_\nu^{-\gamma_k}$. The signal PDF is $S_i=\sum_k w_k S_i^k$ with softmax weights, $n_k=w_k n_s$ and $n_s=\sum_k n_k$; the background $B_i^{\mathrm{S}}$ is uniform in right ascension after signal subtraction, and the test statistic is taken relative to $n_s=0$. Per-segment significance uses $\Delta\ln\mathcal{L}=\ln\mathcal{L}(\hat{n}_k,\hat{\gamma}_k)-\ln\mathcal{L}(n_k=0)$.
assumptions: Each segment is fit with a spatially uniform power law, independent of a predefined neutrino-emission model.
limits: After known detector and ice systematics, statistical uncertainties still dominate.

analysis.reason: Reabsorption of sub-threshold Urca neutrinos removes the resonant bulk-viscous damping of kHz neutron-star-merger oscillations, a quantitative neutrino-transport result for compact remnants that is adjacent to, but not a direct test of, FRB, supernova-engine, or jet models.
analysis.result: An energy-resolved kinetic treatment gives a damping time of 2.7 s for a 1 kHz, 10 km oscillation at nuclear density and 4 MeV, against 19 ms for freely escaping neutrinos. For remnant kHz modes the composition is nearly frozen, so the Urca channel damps them on seconds rather than tens of milliseconds; sampled DD2 states give mean capture energies 19–46 MeV and emission-weighted absorption lengths below 7 m. The kinetic time cannot fall below the transparent resonance minimum $\tau_{\rm res}=2K_{T}B/(C^{2}\omega)$.
analysis.reading_entry: Reabsorbed Urca neutrinos suppress bulk-viscous damping of neutron star merger oscillations
analysis.problem: Transparent Urca bulk viscosity was expected to damp neutron-star-merger density oscillations within tens of milliseconds when the relaxation rate matches the mode frequency, but that estimate treats only thermal-energy neutrinos as free-streaming and omits reabsorption of much harder sub-threshold capture neutrinos.
analysis.method: DD2 $npe\mu$ matter is evolved at fixed cold $\beta$-equilibrium composition with direct Urca from momentum-resolved phase space, modified Urca in the Fermi-surface approximation, and isotropic elastic neutral-current scattering. Linear energy-resolved kinetics define an admittance $\Lambda(\omega,k)$, effective bulk viscosity $\zeta_{\rm eff}(\omega,k)=C^{2}{\rm Re}\Lambda/|-i\omega+B\Lambda|^{2}$, and damping time $\tau=K_T/(\zeta_{\rm eff}\omega^{2})$, using $C=n(\partial\Delta\mu/\partial n)_{T,Y_e,Y_\mu}$, $B=-(\partial\Delta\mu/\partial n_e)_{n,T,Y_\mu}$, and $K_T=n(\partial p/\partial n)_{T,Y_e,Y_\mu}$.
assumptions: Muonic reactions are not included, and the muon fraction is held fixed during the oscillation.
limits: The kinetic damping time cannot be shorter than $\tau_{\rm res}=2K_{T}B/(C^{2}\omega)$, and every computed time lies above that bound.
Rescaling the Urca rates also changes the transparent baseline through its rates and stationary composition $Y_e^{*}$.

S4 Kinetic response: “The kinetic damping time therefore cannot be shorter than $\tau_{\rm res}=2K_{T}B/(C^{2}\omega)$”

analysis.research_progress: Including reabsorption eliminates the transparent resonant window: at the reference states kinetic damping times are about 36–490 times the free-escape baselines (0.43–1.4 s, 2.7–9.7 s, and 19–87 s near $0.5n_0$, $n_0$, and $2n_0$), while sub-threshold neutrinos with $E_{\min}\simeq v_{Fp}\Delta p/(1+v_{Fp})$ are reabsorbed on metre scales, leaving second-scale rather than tens-of-milliseconds Urca damping.

analysis.reason: This directly constrains the circumgalactic contribution to FRB dispersion measure using the second CHIME/FRB baseband catalog, including a radial and mass-dependent DM stack relevant to FRB sightline environments.
analysis.result: Within $D_L\le50\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ and one virial radius, the mean excess is $119\pm44\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$ ($p=0.0053$, about $2.6\sigma$). Across 628 intersections to $150\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, mean DM tentatively declines with impact parameter ($p=0.0046$, about $2.6\sigma$), mainly for $10\le\log(M_*/M_\odot)\le11$. The adopted CGM scaling is $n_e^{\mathrm{CGM}}(r)\propto r^{-3\beta}$, with extrapolated $n_{e,0}=(1.7-21.1)\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ and $\beta=0.68^{+0.15}_{-0.16}$. The excess peaks near $\sim90\pm75\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$ at $0.2\lesssim b_{\min}/r_{\rm CGM}\lesssim0.4$, whereas large-scale structure contributes only about $14\pm39\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$.
analysis.problem: The paper tests whether foreground galaxy CGM halos produce an extragalactic FRB DM excess and whether its radial behavior traces CGM baryons rather than large-scale structure or host-galaxy cross-matching.
analysis.method: BaseCat2 contains 2086 bursts and 1748 independent sources, stacked on foreground halos using $\mathrm{DM}=\int_0^z n_e(z')(1+z')^{-1}dl$ and $\Delta\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{egal}}=\mathrm{DM}-\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{MW}}$. The radial analysis uses $b_{\min}/r_{\rm CGM}$, Gaussian bin-membership weights, and the fit $n_e^{\rm CGM}(r)=n_{e,0}[1+(r/r_c)^2]^{-3\beta/2}$. SLOW and Simba comparisons test alternative contributions, while $\eta_{\mathrm{CGM}}=\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{CGM}}/\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{cosmic}}$ forecasts favorable redshifts.
assumptions: Because DM_CGM and DM_cosmic are drawn from different simulations, they are treated as statistically independent.
limits: The low-impact-parameter extragalactic-DM deficit is likely contaminated by matching FRBs to their own host galaxies.

analysis.reason: The paper quantifies neutrino point-source and stacking detectability of X-ray-bright Seyfert coronae with a global telescope network, which is relevant to compact-object neutrino observations but is not central to FRB, supernova-engine, or jet-breakout work.
analysis.result: In all three scenarios the Circinus Galaxy is by far the brightest southern Seyfert in both neutrinos and MeV $\gamma$-rays. If Seyferts supply the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux up to ${\sim}100\,\mathrm{TeV}$ and Circinus has at least the population-average neutrino luminosity, the IceCube--Baikal-GVD--KM3NeT/ARCA--P-ONE network reaches $5\sigma$ on Circinus by 2038 at the latest; Appendix C gives ${\sim}6.1\sigma$ (NGC 1068-like, $5\sigma$ in 2033) and ${\sim}6.2\sigma$ (average, $5\sigma$ in 2038) by 2040. The scenarios are $(P_{\mathrm{CR}}/P_{\mathrm{th}},\eta)=(0.5,56)$ (NGC 1068-like), $(0.01,1)$ (average), and $(0.5,1)$ (optimistic), with $\eta=B^{2}/\delta B^{2}$. Using NGC 1068 parameters for every source exceeds the TeV diffuse flux by $3.8\sigma$; fitting the flux below ${\sim}100\,\mathrm{TeV}$ instead requires $P_{\mathrm{CR}}/P_{\mathrm{th}}\lesssim 0.05$ and $\eta\lesssim 10$ for most sources. Other nearby Seyferts remain hard to detect individually. For $F_X\ge 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the 2040 optimal stack is $N_{\mathrm{src}}\sim 50$--$70$ with Circinus and ${\sim}100$--$130$ without it.
analysis.problem: Can X-ray-bright Seyfert coronae be discovered as individual neutrino point sources, or only by X-ray-informed stacking, if a hidden coronal origin like NGC 1068 accounts for the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux without accompanying TeV $\gamma$-rays?
analysis.method: Protons are stochastically accelerated in a magnetized corona of size $R_c=r_c R_S$ with $R_S=2GM_{\mathrm{BH}}/c^{2}$, and neutrinos come from photohadronic interactions on coronal X-rays plus hadronuclear interactions; $\gamma$-rays are $\gamma\gamma$-absorbed and emerge mainly at MeV energies. Forecasts use PLE$\nu$M and Asimov data in bins of $\log\hat{E}$ and $\Delta\Psi^{2}=|\hat{\Omega}-\Omega_{\mathrm{src}}|^{2}$, with $\lambda_{ij}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\lambda_{ij}^{\mathrm{astro}}+\lambda_{ij}^{\mathrm{atm}}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\prod_k\mathcal{L}_k$. Each of IceCube, Baikal-GVD, KM3NeT/ARCA, and P-ONE is assigned $1\,\mathrm{km}^{3}$; water detectors are given IceCube-like effective area but better angular resolution for $E_{\nu}\gtrsim 10\,\mathrm{TeV}$ because of the longer Cherenkov-photon scattering length.
assumptions: Water-based neutrino telescopes are expected to achieve better angular resolution than IceCube at high neutrino energies because Cherenkov photons have a longer scattering length.
limits: The optimistic scenario overestimates the neutrino production efficiency of all three sources in the IceCube comparison of NGC 1194, CGCG 164-019, and NGC 7212.
